Verify Now Blog > Copper Keep-out Guidelines for PCB Layout and Component Design Copper Keep-out Guidelines for PCB Layout and Component Design by: Mila Aug 26,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout pcb keepout keep out area in pcb pcb keepout area In modern pcb layout, solid copper pouring is widely used as an optimization technique. However, it is not universally applicable to all components. For devices whose magnetic fields easily couple with PCB copper layers, those with high-low voltage isolation requirements, or those sensitive to parasitic noise, continuous copper under the package can induce extra eddy current loss, EMI problems, or isolation noise coupling. Based on fundamental physical mechanisms, this article explains when to implement a copper keep-out region, layout recommendations for typical components, and common high-frequency design pitfalls. 1. Three Core Mechanisms Requiring Copper Keep-out A component does not automatically require copper clearance beneath it. Applying a pcb keepout depends on component operation, stackup structure, safety standards, EMI targets, and vendor recommendations. Scenario types requiring clearance fall into three categories: Alternating Magnetic Field Coupling → Eddy Current Loss Operating magnetic components generate alternating magnetic fields. When magnetic flux lines penetrate adjacent copper layers, circular eddy currents are induced. These currents cause additional copper loss and temperature rise, while magnetic-eddy interaction degrades EMI performance. Typical components: Common mode chokes, isolation transformers, power inductors, relay coils. High/Low Voltage Isolation → Parasitic Capacitance & Field Coupling Conductive copper extending across an isolation barrier creates parasitic capacitance between high-voltage and low-voltage domains. Under high dv/dt transients or high-frequency common-mode noise, this capacitance acts as a noise path. A poorly designed keep out area in pcb design alters electric field distribution, so isolation requires checking not just physical clearance, but working voltage and transient overvoltage. Typical components: Optocouplers, digital isolators, isolation transformers, high/low voltage interfaces. High dv/dt and di/dt Switching Nodes → Parasitic Noise Coupling Relay contacts and power switches produce rapid voltage/current transients during switching. Rapid transients around high-voltage contacts couple into low-power control circuitry via parasitic capacitance, electromagnetic fields, or shared impedance paths. Defining an explicit pcb keepout area beneath these switching nodes helps minimize parasitic coupling. Typical components: Electromagnetic relays, MOSFETs, IGBTs, high-voltage switching nodes. 2. Component Principles and Keep-out Recommendations Common Mode Chokes Common mode chokes use bifilar winding in the same direction. Differential currents create opposing magnetic flux that cancels out, presenting low impedance. Common-mode currents produce additive flux, generating high impedance to suppress noise. Why Keep-out is Needed: The changing magnetic field around the choke induces eddy currents in underlying copper, causing power loss, heat, and EMI radiation risks. Layout Recommendations: Define the pcb keepout boundary based on the vendor datasheet, extending 1–3 mm beyond the physical outline if necessary (subject to EMI testing). Separate input and output traces according to the filter topology to avoid cross-coupling between filtered and unfiltered sides. Keep sensitive high-speed differential or clock lines away from the choke's magnetic field. Execute an all-layer keep out area in pcb only when explicitly requested by the manufacturer. Isolation and High-Frequency Switching Transformers Transformers rely on alternating magnetic fields between primary and secondary windings for energy transfer and galvanic isolation. Why Keep-out is Needed: Alternating fields induce eddy currents in nearby copper planes, lowering conversion efficiency and disturbing neighboring weak-signal circuits. Layout Recommendations: Partition primary (high-voltage) and secondary (low-voltage) sections, placing a continuous isolation slot without traces crossing it. Minimize power loop areas: keep primary switches and input filter caps close to primary pins; keep secondary filter caps close to secondary pins. Set up a proper pcb keepout area under the transformer body across required layers as specified by the manufacturer, and keep heat-sensitive parts like electrolytic caps away. Optocouplers and Digital Isolators These achieve signal transfer via electrical-to-optical conversion, keeping input and output sides galvanically isolated. Why Keep-out is Needed: Copper extending across the isolation boundary beneath the IC creates parasitic capacitance, compromising noise immunity. Layout Recommendations: Never run copper, traces, or vias directly under the isolation barrier. Maintain required creepage and clearance distances across the split plane. Proper placement in pcb layout demands keeping reference grounds strictly isolated between the primary and secondary domains. Electromagnetic Relays Relays use low-power coils to drive mechanical contacts for high-power loads. Why Keep-out is Needed: Coils produce alternating fields during switching, inducing eddy currents and coupling noise. On the contact side, high-voltage switching creates arc noise and voltage transients that propagate through copper ground planes. Layout Recommendations: Maintain physical distance between low-power coil control traces and high-power contact load traces. Implement an appropriate keep out area in pcb underneath the relay body based on voltage ratings and layer stackup. Add flyback diodes or TVS clamps across DC coils to absorb inductive spikes. 3. General Rules for Copper Clearance Prioritize Datasheets: Always defer to manufacturer guidelines for dimensions and impacted layers before establishing a custom pcb keepout area. Layer-Specific Assessment: If magnetic fields only couple to immediately adjacent copper, clear only those layers. Do not default to removing all inner layers unless required. Hatched Copper is Not a Keep-out Solution: Hatched copper reduces continuous loop area, but eddy currents and parasitic capacitance still exist. It cannot replace a complete copper clear zone. Route Sensitive Signals Away: Never route high-speed clocks or differential pairs directly beneath or through magnetic clearance zones. 4. Common High-Frequency Layout Pitfalls Clearing Top Layer Only: Leaving inner ground planes intact under magnetic components allows eddy currents and parasitic capacitance to persist, ruining EMI compliance. Tight Keep-out Boundaries: Drawing a pcb keepout that exactly hugs the component body leaves zero tolerance, leading to unexpected parasitic coupling near pad edges. Routing High-Speed Lines Under Magnetics: Running clock or differential lines beneath transformers introduces severe jitter and degrades signal integrity. Connecting Isolated Grounds directly: Bridging primary and secondary reference grounds through copper completely defeats galvanic isolation. Relying on Hatched Copper: Assuming copper mesh eliminates magnetic eddy currents is a critical misconception in high-frequency pcb layout. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Copper Keep-out Guidelines for PCB Layout and Component Design Copper Keep-out Guidelines for PCB Layout and Component Design by: Mila Aug 26,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout pcb keepout keep out area in pcb pcb keepout area In modern pcb layout, solid copper pouring is widely used as an optimization technique. However, it is not universally applicable to all components. For devices whose magnetic fields easily couple with PCB copper layers, those with high-low voltage isolation requirements, or those sensitive to parasitic noise, continuous copper under the package can induce extra eddy current loss, EMI problems, or isolation noise coupling. Based on fundamental physical mechanisms, this article explains when to implement a copper keep-out region, layout recommendations for typical components, and common high-frequency design pitfalls. 1. Three Core Mechanisms Requiring Copper Keep-out A component does not automatically require copper clearance beneath it. Applying a pcb keepout depends on component operation, stackup structure, safety standards, EMI targets, and vendor recommendations. Scenario types requiring clearance fall into three categories: Alternating Magnetic Field Coupling → Eddy Current Loss Operating magnetic components generate alternating magnetic fields. When magnetic flux lines penetrate adjacent copper layers, circular eddy currents are induced. These currents cause additional copper loss and temperature rise, while magnetic-eddy interaction degrades EMI performance. Typical components: Common mode chokes, isolation transformers, power inductors, relay coils. High/Low Voltage Isolation → Parasitic Capacitance & Field Coupling Conductive copper extending across an isolation barrier creates parasitic capacitance between high-voltage and low-voltage domains. Under high dv/dt transients or high-frequency common-mode noise, this capacitance acts as a noise path. A poorly designed keep out area in pcb design alters electric field distribution, so isolation requires checking not just physical clearance, but working voltage and transient overvoltage. Typical components: Optocouplers, digital isolators, isolation transformers, high/low voltage interfaces. High dv/dt and di/dt Switching Nodes → Parasitic Noise Coupling Relay contacts and power switches produce rapid voltage/current transients during switching. Rapid transients around high-voltage contacts couple into low-power control circuitry via parasitic capacitance, electromagnetic fields, or shared impedance paths. Defining an explicit pcb keepout area beneath these switching nodes helps minimize parasitic coupling. Typical components: Electromagnetic relays, MOSFETs, IGBTs, high-voltage switching nodes. 2. Component Principles and Keep-out Recommendations Common Mode Chokes Common mode chokes use bifilar winding in the same direction. Differential currents create opposing magnetic flux that cancels out, presenting low impedance. Common-mode currents produce additive flux, generating high impedance to suppress noise. Why Keep-out is Needed: The changing magnetic field around the choke induces eddy currents in underlying copper, causing power loss, heat, and EMI radiation risks. Layout Recommendations: Define the pcb keepout boundary based on the vendor datasheet, extending 1–3 mm beyond the physical outline if necessary (subject to EMI testing). Separate input and output traces according to the filter topology to avoid cross-coupling between filtered and unfiltered sides. Keep sensitive high-speed differential or clock lines away from the choke's magnetic field. Execute an all-layer keep out area in pcb only when explicitly requested by the manufacturer. Isolation and High-Frequency Switching Transformers Transformers rely on alternating magnetic fields between primary and secondary windings for energy transfer and galvanic isolation. Why Keep-out is Needed: Alternating fields induce eddy currents in nearby copper planes, lowering conversion efficiency and disturbing neighboring weak-signal circuits. Layout Recommendations: Partition primary (high-voltage) and secondary (low-voltage) sections, placing a continuous isolation slot without traces crossing it. Minimize power loop areas: keep primary switches and input filter caps close to primary pins; keep secondary filter caps close to secondary pins. Set up a proper pcb keepout area under the transformer body across required layers as specified by the manufacturer, and keep heat-sensitive parts like electrolytic caps away. Optocouplers and Digital Isolators These achieve signal transfer via electrical-to-optical conversion, keeping input and output sides galvanically isolated. Why Keep-out is Needed: Copper extending across the isolation boundary beneath the IC creates parasitic capacitance, compromising noise immunity. Layout Recommendations: Never run copper, traces, or vias directly under the isolation barrier. Maintain required creepage and clearance distances across the split plane. Proper placement in pcb layout demands keeping reference grounds strictly isolated between the primary and secondary domains. Electromagnetic Relays Relays use low-power coils to drive mechanical contacts for high-power loads. Why Keep-out is Needed: Coils produce alternating fields during switching, inducing eddy currents and coupling noise. On the contact side, high-voltage switching creates arc noise and voltage transients that propagate through copper ground planes. Layout Recommendations: Maintain physical distance between low-power coil control traces and high-power contact load traces. Implement an appropriate keep out area in pcb underneath the relay body based on voltage ratings and layer stackup. Add flyback diodes or TVS clamps across DC coils to absorb inductive spikes. 3. General Rules for Copper Clearance Prioritize Datasheets: Always defer to manufacturer guidelines for dimensions and impacted layers before establishing a custom pcb keepout area. Layer-Specific Assessment: If magnetic fields only couple to immediately adjacent copper, clear only those layers. Do not default to removing all inner layers unless required. Hatched Copper is Not a Keep-out Solution: Hatched copper reduces continuous loop area, but eddy currents and parasitic capacitance still exist. It cannot replace a complete copper clear zone. Route Sensitive Signals Away: Never route high-speed clocks or differential pairs directly beneath or through magnetic clearance zones. 4. Common High-Frequency Layout Pitfalls Clearing Top Layer Only: Leaving inner ground planes intact under magnetic components allows eddy currents and parasitic capacitance to persist, ruining EMI compliance. Tight Keep-out Boundaries: Drawing a pcb keepout that exactly hugs the component body leaves zero tolerance, leading to unexpected parasitic coupling near pad edges. Routing High-Speed Lines Under Magnetics: Running clock or differential lines beneath transformers introduces severe jitter and degrades signal integrity. Connecting Isolated Grounds directly: Bridging primary and secondary reference grounds through copper completely defeats galvanic isolation. Relying on Hatched Copper: Assuming copper mesh eliminates magnetic eddy currents is a critical misconception in high-frequency pcb layout. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Ground Stitching Vias in High-Speed PCB Differential Via Design Ground Stitching Vias in High-Speed PCB Differential Via Design by: Mila Aug 25,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout stitching vias differential via design high speed pcb high speed board design In high speed PCB debugging, engineers frequently encounter high-speed link communications failure, severe eye diagram jitter, TDR impedance anomalies near via regions, and EMI radiation exceeding limits by several dBs. After verifying the schematic and trace impedance control, the root cause is often identified: a lack of dedicated stitching vias adjacent to the differential signal vias. 1. Why Return Paths Matter in High Speed Board Design When a signal current flows from the driver to the receiver along a transmission line, an equal and opposite return current travels back through the reference plane. At high frequencies, return current naturally concentrates directly beneath the signal trace to minimize the current loop area. Together, the signal and return currents form a closed loop. A smaller loop area yields lower parasitic inductance, improved signal integrity, and significantly lower EMI radiation. In high speed board design, when a signal transitions between layers or crosses a split plane, maintaining a continuous, minimal return path is essential. (Signal Current + Return Current) 2. How Layer Transitions Disrupt Return Paths When a signal transitions between layers through a via, its reference planes may change, requiring a vertical path for the return current. For instance, if a signal references L2 before a transition and L3 after, the signal current jumps via the signal via. Without stitching vias nearby, no low-impedance vertical bridge exists between L2 and L3. The return current must detour across the reference plane to find a distant ground via, expanding the loop area. This detour leads to three major issues: Higher Parasitic Inductance: Increases loop inductance and degrades high-frequency performance. Impedance Discontinuities: Exacerbates reflections, resulting in ringing and eye diagram degradation. Elevated EMI: Large current loops act as efficient antennas, raising EMI risks. 3. Restoring Return Paths with Stitching Vias Placing stitching vias adjacent to signal vias creates a short, low-impedance vertical path between reference planes. The return current transitions locally through these ground vias rather than taking long detours, maintaining a compact current loop. Ground stitching vias can be through-hole, blind, or buried vias, provided they reliably tie the relevant reference planes together. 4. The Impact of Anti-Pads on Return Current To reduce parasitic capacitance and improve impedance matching, anti-pads are etched into reference planes around signal vias. While anti-pads raise local impedance toward the target (such as 50Ω or 100Ω), excessively large anti-pads remove copper under the via field, forcing the return path outward and increasing loop inductance. Balancing anti-pad sizing with return path continuity is critical in differential via design. 5. Placement Strategies for Stitching Vias Near Anti-Pads Whether addressing plane swaps or anti-pad voids, the objective remains minimizing return path length. Stitching vias should be positioned on the continuous ground copper outside the anti-pad perimeter, rather than inside the void, to ensure immediate vertical coupling for return currents. 6. Key Rules for Differential Via Design in High Speed PCBs Spacing and Pitch: Place stitching vias close to signal vias to maintain path continuity. While a 50-mil pitch serves as a loose rule of thumb for standard rates, ultra-high-speed interfaces (like PCIe 5.0/6.0 or 112G PAM4) demand tighter spacing (often 20–30 mil) validated by SI simulation. Symmetry and Quantity: Place stitching vias symmetrically around differential pairs to mitigate mode conversion ($S_{CD21}$) and absorb common-mode noise. High-speed links may require multiple ground vias forming a via fence around the pair. Layer Connectivity Verification: Confirm that ground vias connect the exact reference layers involved in the transition. Stub Management: Via stubs create parasitic resonance. For high-bandwidth channels, use backdrilling or blind/buried vias to minimize stub lengths. 7.Design Checklist Near-by stitching vias are present at all signal layer transitions. Ground vias correctly bridge the corresponding upper and lower reference planes. Stitching vias are placed symmetrically around differential via pairs. Ground vias sit on solid copper outside the signal via anti-pad voids. Anti-pad dimensions balance via impedance tuning without excessive copper removal. Ultra-high-speed differential links are verified via SI simulations for impedance, return path continuity, and mode conversion. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Ground Stitching Vias in High-Speed PCB Differential Via Design Ground Stitching Vias in High-Speed PCB Differential Via Design by: Mila Aug 25,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout stitching vias differential via design high speed pcb high speed board design In high speed PCB debugging, engineers frequently encounter high-speed link communications failure, severe eye diagram jitter, TDR impedance anomalies near via regions, and EMI radiation exceeding limits by several dBs. After verifying the schematic and trace impedance control, the root cause is often identified: a lack of dedicated stitching vias adjacent to the differential signal vias. 1. Why Return Paths Matter in High Speed Board Design When a signal current flows from the driver to the receiver along a transmission line, an equal and opposite return current travels back through the reference plane. At high frequencies, return current naturally concentrates directly beneath the signal trace to minimize the current loop area. Together, the signal and return currents form a closed loop. A smaller loop area yields lower parasitic inductance, improved signal integrity, and significantly lower EMI radiation. In high speed board design, when a signal transitions between layers or crosses a split plane, maintaining a continuous, minimal return path is essential. (Signal Current + Return Current) 2. How Layer Transitions Disrupt Return Paths When a signal transitions between layers through a via, its reference planes may change, requiring a vertical path for the return current. For instance, if a signal references L2 before a transition and L3 after, the signal current jumps via the signal via. Without stitching vias nearby, no low-impedance vertical bridge exists between L2 and L3. The return current must detour across the reference plane to find a distant ground via, expanding the loop area. This detour leads to three major issues: Higher Parasitic Inductance: Increases loop inductance and degrades high-frequency performance. Impedance Discontinuities: Exacerbates reflections, resulting in ringing and eye diagram degradation. Elevated EMI: Large current loops act as efficient antennas, raising EMI risks. 3. Restoring Return Paths with Stitching Vias Placing stitching vias adjacent to signal vias creates a short, low-impedance vertical path between reference planes. The return current transitions locally through these ground vias rather than taking long detours, maintaining a compact current loop. Ground stitching vias can be through-hole, blind, or buried vias, provided they reliably tie the relevant reference planes together. 4. The Impact of Anti-Pads on Return Current To reduce parasitic capacitance and improve impedance matching, anti-pads are etched into reference planes around signal vias. While anti-pads raise local impedance toward the target (such as 50Ω or 100Ω), excessively large anti-pads remove copper under the via field, forcing the return path outward and increasing loop inductance. Balancing anti-pad sizing with return path continuity is critical in differential via design. 5. Placement Strategies for Stitching Vias Near Anti-Pads Whether addressing plane swaps or anti-pad voids, the objective remains minimizing return path length. Stitching vias should be positioned on the continuous ground copper outside the anti-pad perimeter, rather than inside the void, to ensure immediate vertical coupling for return currents. 6. Key Rules for Differential Via Design in High Speed PCBs Spacing and Pitch: Place stitching vias close to signal vias to maintain path continuity. While a 50-mil pitch serves as a loose rule of thumb for standard rates, ultra-high-speed interfaces (like PCIe 5.0/6.0 or 112G PAM4) demand tighter spacing (often 20–30 mil) validated by SI simulation. Symmetry and Quantity: Place stitching vias symmetrically around differential pairs to mitigate mode conversion ($S_{CD21}$) and absorb common-mode noise. High-speed links may require multiple ground vias forming a via fence around the pair. Layer Connectivity Verification: Confirm that ground vias connect the exact reference layers involved in the transition. Stub Management: Via stubs create parasitic resonance. For high-bandwidth channels, use backdrilling or blind/buried vias to minimize stub lengths. 7.Design Checklist Near-by stitching vias are present at all signal layer transitions. Ground vias correctly bridge the corresponding upper and lower reference planes. Stitching vias are placed symmetrically around differential via pairs. Ground vias sit on solid copper outside the signal via anti-pad voids. Anti-pad dimensions balance via impedance tuning without excessive copper removal. Ultra-high-speed differential links are verified via SI simulations for impedance, return path continuity, and mode conversion. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Guide to Selecting and Placing RF Components in RF PCB Layout Guide to Selecting and Placing RF Components in RF PCB Layout by: Mila Aug 14,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout rf pcb rf component rf design rf pcb layout rf pcb layout guidelines In RF PCB design, selecting and placing the right RF components is critical to signal integrity, impedance matching, and electromagnetic isolation. Because RF signals are highly sensitive to trace length, grounding, and impedance discontinuities, even small layout changes can affect overall circuit performance. This guide covers key RF PCB layout principles for component placement, parasitic control, connector selection, and thermal management. For a broader introduction to RF PCB design, see our RF PCB Design Guide . 1. Why RF Component Placement Matters in RF PCB Design At high frequencies, PCB traces no longer behave simply as conductors but exhibit transmission-line characteristics. When the electrical length of a trace becomes significant relative to the signal transition time, the PCB trace needs to be treated as a transmission line. Under these conditions, impedance discontinuities, discontinuities in the reference plane, and excessively long signal paths can cause reflections, crosstalk, and electromagnetic radiation. An improper RF PCB layout can lead to several common problems: Increased insertion loss: Long signal paths or impedance discontinuities can reduce power-transfer efficiency. Increased electromagnetic interference: Insufficient isolation between components can allow nearby signals to couple into sensitive circuits. Reduced frequency stability: Oscillators and other timing components can experience frequency drift and increased phase noise when exposed to interference. Worsened parasitic effects: Vias, pads, and traces introduce additional parasitic inductance and capacitance, potentially detuning the circuit. Localized overheating: Poor thermal paths around power amplifiers and other high-power components can reduce performance or even cause device failure. Many of these problems originate from component placement decisions made early in the design process. Establishing clear placement principles during the RF design stage can significantly reduce debugging effort and shorten the overall product development cycle. 2. Active RF Component Selection and Placement Active components are at the core of an RF circuit and include low-noise amplifiers, oscillators, mixers, and other RF devices. Because these components are highly sensitive to their electrical and electromagnetic environment, their selection and placement should follow carefully defined design requirements. Low-Noise Amplifiers: Balancing Noise Figure and Linearity An amplifier located at the front end of an RF receive chain has a direct impact on receiver sensitivity. When selecting an RF component, three key parameters should be considered: In an RF PCB layout, the matching network should be designed according to the device port characteristics and S-parameters to achieve the appropriate impedance match, maximize power transfer, and minimize reflections. Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as possible to the device power pins to minimize the current-loop area and parasitic inductance. Oscillators: Maintaining Frequency Stability Oscillators and frequency sources provide stable reference or local-oscillator signals for RF systems. Their frequency stability, phase noise, and sensitivity to power-supply noise can all have a direct impact on system performance. The key oscillator placement principles in an RF PCB layout include: Place close to the corresponding clock or RF pins: Minimize signal-path length to reduce parasitic effects and external noise coupling. Provide a continuous ground reference: Keep a continuous ground plane beneath the device and follow the manufacturer's recommended footprint and layout whenever available. Keep away from interference sources: Switching digital circuits, high-current loops, and switching power supplies should be separated from the oscillator area. Maintain isolation from antenna feed lines: High-frequency oscillators should be kept away from antenna feed lines, with shielding added when necessary. Provide a clean power supply: VCO and PLL circuits should use appropriate low-ESR decoupling capacitors to suppress power-supply noise. In practical RF design, properly placing the oscillator and separating it from radiating sources such as inductors and switching power supplies can significantly reduce EMI. This is particularly important in applications such as medical and industrial equipment, where electromagnetic compatibility requirements are stringent. Mixers: Optimizing Frequency Conversion Mixers perform frequency conversion between RF, LO, and IF signals. Conversion loss, port isolation, and linearity are among their key performance parameters. Mixers are particularly sensitive to PCB layout because improper routing can cause local-oscillator leakage into the RF or IF paths. Key RF design considerations for mixer placement include: Keep the local oscillator (LO) trace as short as practical and away from sensitive RF and IF signal paths. Place baluns and matching networks close to the corresponding mixer ports to maintain impedance continuity. Use ground-via fences and stitching vias around the mixer area to improve isolation and suppress unwanted radiation. Maintain physical separation between the three ports and avoid parallel routing that could increase signal coupling. 3. Passive RF Component Placement Optimization Passive components perform critical functions such as impedance matching, filtering, and power decoupling in RF circuits. Their selection and placement can have an equally significant impact on overall circuit performance. Capacitor Selection and Placement The impedance of a capacitor varies with frequency. Because practical capacitors contain parasitic inductance, their impedance reaches a minimum around the self-resonant frequency (SRF) and then increases as the frequency rises beyond the SRF. Therefore, when selecting an RF component, capacitors should be chosen based on their impedance characteristics over the target operating frequency range, while taking PCB and package parasitics into account. Key capacitor placement recommendations include: Prefer NP0/C0G capacitors for applications requiring high temperature stability and good high-frequency performance. Choose decoupling capacitors for the target frequency range and PDN impedance, and keep the connections to power pins short. Place decoupling capacitors as close as possible to the device power pins to minimize the current-loop area. Avoid routing between the device and its reference ground plane so that the grounding path remains as short as possible. Inductor and Balun Placement Inductors, baluns, and other magnetic components can generate stray magnetic fields and may also be susceptible to external magnetic interference. In RF PCB layout, these components should generally be placed close to the relevant RF ports to minimize connection length. Their orientation should also be considered to reduce unwanted magnetic coupling between adjacent components. For high-Q inductors, avoid routing unrelated signal traces underneath the component whenever possible. Prioritizing High-Q Components Quality factor, or Q, is an important parameter for RF passive components. In RF passive networks such as matching networks, resonant circuits, and filters, a higher Q generally means lower passive loss and better selectivity. However, actual performance also depends on component construction, operating frequency, and circuit topology. For RF design applications, high-Q passive components should therefore be considered for critical locations such as matching networks, resonant circuits, and filters. 4. Controlling Parasitic Effects: A Core RF PCB Layout Challenge Parasitic parameters are one of the hidden challenges in RF design. Pads, vias, and traces all introduce additional inductance and capacitance, which can cause actual circuit performance to deviate from simulation results. Effective parasitic control is therefore an important part of RF PCB layout. Reducing Parasitic Inductance in Traces and Pads Long and narrow current paths can introduce significant parasitic inductance and degrade high-frequency performance. Recommended measures include: Minimize RF signal-path length and use a compact component arrangement. Use an appropriate trace width and reduce inductance as far as the controlled-impedance requirements allow. Keep the connection between decoupling capacitors and power pins as short as possible. Controlling Via-Stub Resonance A conventional through-via can form a stub when it extends through unused PCB layers. At sufficiently high frequencies, this unused section can behave as a resonant structure and introduce additional reflection and loss. Possible solutions include: Use blind or buried vias for critical high-frequency transitions when appropriate to eliminate unnecessary via stubs. When blind or buried vias are not practical, use back-drilling to remove excess via stubs. Minimize the number of vias in critical RF signal paths. The appropriate solution depends on the operating frequency, stackup, electrical length of the via stub, fabrication capabilities, and overall cost requirements. Minimizing Ground-Loop Area An incomplete or excessively long ground-return path increases loop inductance and can aggravate electromagnetic radiation. Recommended practices include: Maintain a continuous ground plane and avoid unnecessary slots or splits in the RF return path. Use distributed ground stitching vias to connect ground planes across PCB layers. Determine ground-via-fence spacing based on operating frequency, PCB stackup, shielding requirements, and manufacturing capability. The primary purpose of stitching vias is to provide a low-impedance return path and help suppress unwanted plane resonances. As operating frequency increases, via density generally needs to increase accordingly, with additional stitching vias used around critical signal transitions and isolation boundaries. Many of these issues are also related to common RF PCB layout mistakes, such as excessive vias, discontinuous ground planes, and poorly placed matching networks. For more examples, see our guide to common RF PCB layout mistakes and how to avoid them . 5. High-Frequency Connector Selection and Placement Connectors provide the interface through which RF signals enter and leave the PCB. An unsuitable connector or poor connector layout can become a performance bottleneck in the entire RF signal chain. Key Connector Selection Criteria During RF component selection, connectors should meet the following requirements: Characteristic impedance should match the transmission-line impedance, commonly 50 Ω or 75 Ω depending on the application. The operating frequency range should cover the required RF band. Rated power and voltage should meet system requirements to prevent excessive heating or dielectric breakdown. Mechanical dimensions should be compatible with the PCB layout without interfering with nearby components. Mating-cycle requirements should be consistent with the expected product lifetime. Connector Placement Considerations In an RF PCB layout, connector placement should consider the following: Maintain an appropriate ground reference beneath and around the connector to provide a low-impedance return path. Ensure a smooth transition from the connector signal pin to the PCB transmission line to minimize impedance discontinuities. Connect the outer shell of coaxial connectors to the ground plane with multiple ground vias to improve the return path and mechanical/electrical connection. For board-to-board RF connectors, maintain proper alignment and follow the connector manufacturer's recommended layout to minimize signal degradation. Common connector types can be categorized as wire-to-wire, board-to-board, and wire-to-board connectors, each serving different application requirements. For RF applications, connector selection should focus on characteristic impedance, operating frequency, insertion loss, return loss, crosstalk, mechanical structure, and other relevant electrical and mechanical parameters. 6. RF PCB Thermal Management RF power devices can generate significant heat during operation. Inadequate thermal design can lead to parameter drift, reduced component lifetime, or even device failure. Effective thermal management strategies include: Thermal via arrays: Use thermal vias beneath the exposed pad to transfer heat to internal copper planes, with size and spacing optimized for the package and power dissipation. Thermal pad design: Connect the exposed pad on the bottom of the device to a sufficiently large copper area to increase the effective heat-spreading area. Metal heat sinks: For high-power devices, add a heat sink with an appropriate thermal interface material between the device and heat sink. Airflow planning: Reserve sufficient ventilation space around heat sinks and use fans when necessary to improve forced-air cooling. Internal copper planes: Use continuous internal copper planes as heat-spreading layers to distribute heat and reduce localized temperature rise. Proper RF component selection and placement are essential for maintaining signal integrity, impedance continuity, isolation, and thermal performance. By following practical RF PCB layout principles from the early design stage, engineers can reduce parasitic effects, minimize signal loss, and improve overall RF system reliability. Verify Now Blog > HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design by: Mila Sep 03,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hdi pcb HDI pcb design optical module pcb high speed pcb layout An optical module PCB is a typical high-frequency, high-density HDI PCB precision board. Its material selection is closely related to transmission rate, link length, loss budget, and device platforms. While 10G and lower modules can use materials like high-Tg FR-4, high-speed modules operating at 25G, 56G, 100G, 400G, and 800G impose stringent requirements on low-loss materials, impedance control, and manufacturing consistency. Below are seven core layout design points and key differences compared to standard PCBs, focusing on high speed pcb layout and practical signal integrity engineering without rigid design fallacies. 1. Substrate Selection and StackUp Design Substrate selection and layer stackup form the foundation for stable high-frequency transmission, directly determining link insertion loss, impedance accuracy, and signal integrity. Multi-Dimensional Rate-Matched Selection: For 25G+ channels, select substrates considering Nyquist frequency, link length, insertion loss budget, dielectric loss, copper foil roughness, and stackup. For long-distance or low-loss channels, choose mid-to-low loss high-speed substrates. Non-critical areas like low-speed control and power can use high-Tg FR-4 to balance performance and cost on an optical module PCB. Adjacent Reference Ground Planes: High-speed differential signal layers should adopt a "signal-reference ground" structure to minimize edge-field coupling. Power layers should pair with adjacent ground layers to optimize PDN impedance via inter-layer capacitance. Pre-Simulation Impedance Modeling: Determine stackup parameters early through SI simulation. Power Integrity (PI) Optimization Focus on low-impedance return paths, minimal current loops, and sub-region noise reduction. Minimal Loop Decoupling: Configure decoupling networks based on target PDN impedance. Place capacitors close to power pins to minimize parasitic inductance. Solid Ground Plane Priority: Maintain a continuous, low-impedance ground plane across the HDI PCB to provide a solid reference. Apply localized filtering for sensitive analog zones rather than single-point star grounding across the board. Thermal Copper Pour for Power Chips: Place large copper areas with thermal via arrays beneath heat-generating components like laser drivers to disperse heat quickly. 5. Thermal Management in HDI PCB Design Optical module DSPs, optical drivers, and laser diodes generate concentrated heat. High temperatures cause device aging, DK/Df parameter drift, and impedance shifts. Efficient Thermal Paths: Place dense thermal via arrays under high-power devices (DSP, TOSA) to transfer heat from the optical module PCB inner layers to the metal housing. Hot/Cold Component Partitioning: Isolate heat sources from temperature-sensitive optical and clock components to prevent thermal drift and premature aging. Symmetrical Design against Warpage: Balance copper distribution and layer stack-ups across the HDI PCB to manage thermal-mechanical stress during reflow soldering. （Thermal Path IC → Thermal Via → Copper Plane → Housing） 6. EMC and Grounding for High Speed PCB Layout Symmetrical Routing for Common-Mode Noise: Maintain structural symmetry in high-speed differential traces to reduce EMI radiation. Connect the module metal shell to the PCB ground for low-impedance shielding. Interface ESD Protection : Place TVS diodes and common-mode chokes near edge connectors to route ESD currents quickly to chassis ground. Isolate Interference Sources: Keep power inductors and switching regulators away from sensitive RX analog inputs to prevent magnetic coupling. 7. DFM Guidelines for Optical Module PCB Manufacturing Precise HDI pcb design and assembly standards ensure manufacturing yield for dense components. Precision Soldering Design: Use Via-in-Pad or micro-vias for high-density BGAs. For QFN thermal pads, use segmented stencil openings to reduce solder voiding and floating. Optical Alignment Tolerance: Match mechanical outline and mounting hole tolerances precisely with metal housings to avoid optical misalignments. Test Points and Gold Fingers: Keep test points off high-speed trunk lines. Use hard gold plating for edge connector gold fingers to ensure durability across insertion cycles. 8.Optical Module PCB vs Standard PCB Core Differences Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > High Speed PCB Design Guidelines for Impedance and SI High Speed PCB Design Guidelines for Impedance and SI by: Mila Aug 24,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb design high speed PCB design High-performance board layout is not merely about transmitting signals faster—it is about ensuring they remain stable, continuous, and predictable throughout the entire channel. As edge rates push into the sub-nanosecond range, traces begin to act like transmission lines. Impedance discontinuities, fragmented reference planes, and extended loop paths can quickly lead to reflections, crosstalk, and unwanted electromagnetic interference (EMI). To mitigate these signal integrity (SI) issues, engineers must take a systematic approach across three critical pillars: impedance matching, layer stackup architecture, and signal return management. 1. Impedance Control: Preserving Signal Continuity Lumped Circuit vs. Transmission Line Impedance It is vital to distinguish general circuit impedance from transmission line characteristic impedance (Z 0 ): Lumped Circuit Impedance: Frequency-dependent (f), composed of resistance (R), inductive reactance （XL=2πfL）, and capacitive reactance（XC=1/2πfC）. Characteristic Impedance (Z 0 ): A distributed property determined by the trace geometry and dielectric parameters. For an ideal, lossless line: Where L 0 and C 0 represent distributed inductance and capacitance per unit length. In an ideal scenario, Z 0 remains constant regardless of signal frequency. Why Impedance Matching Matters When signal edges become extremely sharp (such as DDR4 clocks at 2400–3200 MHz), impedance mismatches trigger reflections. These reflections cause ringing, consume timing jitter budget, and can ultimately lead to bit errors. Most high-speed link failures—such as closed eye diagrams on USB 3.0, PCIe, or SerDes interfaces—stem from unmanaged impedance variations rather than schematic flaws. Transmission Line Architectures Analytical Equations & Physical Trends Single-ended impedance calculations provide clear design levers: Microstrip: Stripline: (Where Z 0 = Target Impedance [e.g., 50Ω], $\varepsilon_r$ = Relative Permittivity, $H$ = Dielectric Height, $W$ = Trace Width, $T$ = Copper Thickness) Physical Relationships: Directly Proportional: Z₀ ∝ H (Greater height reduces parasitic capacitance, increasing impedance). Inversely Proportional: Z₀ ∝ 1/W, 1/T, 1/εr (Wider traces, thicker copper, or higher εr boost capacitance, lowering impedance). In practice, field solvers like Polar Si9000 are used to calculate precise trace geometry based on stackup specifications. Manufacturing Tolerances Standard fabrication typically guarantees a ±10% impedance tolerance (45Ω-55Ω for a nominal 50Ω line). While sufficient for lower data rates, ultra-high-speed SerDes operating at 10+ Gbps have very tight noise margins. In these critical channels, tightening tolerances to ±5% or ±3% helps prevent channel loss and reflection from closing the eye pattern. 2. Stackup Planning: Structuring the Board Architecture The Role of Layer Stackup Layer stackup defines the physical foundation of the PCB. It assigns signal, power, and ground layers to establish clear signal reference paths, manage power delivery network (PDN) impedance, and ensure inter-layer isolation. Common Layer Architectures Signal and Reference Rules Adjacent Reference: Place critical signal layers directly adjacent to continuous reference planes (GND preferred) to minimize loop inductance. Orthogonal Routing: Route adjacent signal layers perpendicularly to eliminate broadside broadside crosstalk. Avoid Split Planes: Never route critical traces across plane splits. If a signal must cross a split, avoid using large 100 pF–1 nF capacitors—their low Self-Resonant Frequency (SRF) makes them inductive at GHz frequencies. Instead, use high-SRF 0.5 pF–10 pF RF stitching capacitors directly at the crossing to preserve a low-impedance path. 3. Signal Return Paths: Managing High-Frequency Currents Minimum Inductance Rule Every signal travels in a closed loop consisting of a forward path and a return path. While DC current follows the path of least resistance, high-frequency AC current strictly follows the path of least inductance. Consequently, return currents naturally flow on the reference plane directly beneath the signal trace. High-Frequency Return Characteristics Gaussian Current Profile: Return current spreads out in a Gaussian distribution centered directly under the trace. Thicker dielectrics widen this distribution; therefore, maintaining 3W/5W clearance from plane edges is crucial to prevent field truncation and EMI emissions. Edge Rate Sensitivity: Sharper rise times concentrate return current tighter beneath the trace, increasing the need for uninterrupted reference copper. Mitigating Return Loop Disruption Crossing a reference gap forces return current to detour around the obstacle, creating three distinct issues: Extended loop paths that dramatically increase loop inductance. Localized impedance drops that trigger signal reflections and ringing. Expanded loop area, radiating energy and risking EMC failure. Layout Optimization Rules Continuous Reference: Keep critical traces over solid, un-split ground copper wherever possible. Stitching Vias for Layer Transitions: When single-ended signals switch reference layers, place a ground stitching via nearby (ideally within 3W) to allow return current to hop cleanly between ground planes. Differential Pair Self-Referencing: Differential signals (PCIe, HDMI, Ethernet) rely primarily on odd-mode coupling between the pair for return current. They do not require 1:1 ground via placement at every layer transition. Place ground vias near differential pairs for shielding and PDN control without overcrowding the BGA breakout area. Verify Now Blog > How to Design an H-Bridge Motor Driver: Circuit & PCB Layout Guide How to Design an H-Bridge Motor Driver: Circuit & PCB Layout Guide by: Mila Aug 17,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout h bridge motor driver h bridge drive circuit dc motor design dc motor driver design 1. Overview of H-Bridge Drive Circuits An H-bridge drive circuit is one of the most widely used basic topologies in DC motor drive systems. Its core structure consists of four independently controlled MOSFETs arranged as a bridge. By controlling different switching combinations, the circuit can control the current direction and achieve forward rotation, reverse rotation, speed control, and braking of a DC motor. The topology resembles the letter “H,” which is where the name H-bridge comes from. This article provides a systematic analysis of the key considerations in H-bridge circuit design, covering device characteristics, high-side driving principles, bootstrap circuit design, and PCB Layout guidelines. It focuses on the essential aspects from circuit design to board-level implementation, providing practical guidance for DC motor driver design and optimization. (H-Bridge Circuit Topology) 2. Key Device Characteristics and Selection 2.1 MOSFET Body Diode Characteristics Inside an N-channel power MOSFET, the source and drain are N-type semiconductor regions, while the body region is made of P-type semiconductor material. This structure forms two PN junctions. Since the source is normally shorted to the body, the source-body PN junction remains at zero bias and does not function as a diode. Only the drain-body PN junction operates normally, forming the built-in body diode. This characteristic is common to power MOSFETs and is also the physical basis for the reverse-parallel diode shown in MOSFET symbols used in circuit simulation models. 2.2 Function and Selection of Freewheeling Diodes A DC motor is a typical inductive load, meaning that its current cannot change instantaneously. When the MOSFETs in an H-bridge switch rapidly between states, sudden changes in the motor winding current can generate high-voltage back-EMF spikes, which may damage the MOSFETs or cause abnormal circuit operation. A freewheeling diode is connected in parallel with the MOSFET drain and source. Its main functions include: Providing a freewheeling path: When the MOSFET turns off, the diode provides a closed-loop path for the residual current in the motor winding, preventing high-voltage spikes caused by forced current interruption. Protecting the devices from overvoltage: The diode clamps the back-EMF amplitude and isolates the power devices from voltage spikes, reducing the risk of device damage. Improving electromagnetic performance: In high-frequency switching applications, the diode helps suppress electromagnetic interference (EMI), reduce operating noise, and improve system stability. The MOSFET's built-in body diode can provide basic freewheeling functionality, but its relatively high forward voltage, long reverse-recovery time, and slow switching response make it unsuitable for high-frequency and high-current applications. In practical designs, an external Schottky diode is commonly connected in parallel as a dedicated freewheeling device. Its short reverse-recovery time and low forward voltage can significantly reduce freewheeling losses and improve circuit reliability. (Freewheeling diode connected in parallel with an upper-arm MOSFET) 2.3 Key MOSFET Selection Parameters When selecting power MOSFETs for an H-bridge motor driver, four parameters should be considered carefully: Drain-source breakdown voltage (VDS): The rating should be 1.5 to 2 times higher than the supply voltage to provide sufficient safety margin for back-EMF spikes. Continuous drain current (ID): The rating should exceed both the motor's rated current and stall current, with additional margin based on the thermal design. On-resistance (RDS(on)): This parameter directly determines conduction losses and device heating. For MOSFETs with the same voltage rating, a lower RDS(on) generally results in higher system efficiency. Gate charge (Qg): This parameter reflects MOSFET switching characteristics. A lower Qg generally results in lower switching losses, but it must be properly matched to the driving capability of the gate driver IC. 3. High-Side Driving and Bootstrap Circuit Design 3.1 Differences Between High-Side and Low-Side Driving Based on their positions in the H-bridge topology, MOSFETs can be divided into high-side and low-side devices. The high-side MOSFET is connected between the power supply and the load, while the low-side MOSFET is connected between the load and ground. The fundamental condition for turning on a MOSFET is that the gate-source voltage must exceed its threshold voltage: VGS > VGS(th) The source of a low-side MOSFET is connected to ground, so its potential remains fixed. Applying the appropriate drive voltage to the gate is therefore sufficient to turn it on, making the drive circuit relatively simple. The source of a high-side MOSFET is connected to the load. Its potential changes dynamically with the switching state and remains above ground. As a result, a conventional drive voltage cannot provide sufficient gate-source voltage. A dedicated circuit is required to generate a gate-drive voltage higher than the supply voltage. A bootstrap circuit is currently one of the most common low-cost solutions for high-side MOSFET driving. 3.2 How the Bootstrap Circuit Works A bootstrap circuit consists of a bootstrap diode and a bootstrap capacitor and operates together with the gate driver IC. Taking a half-bridge topology as an example, its operation can be divided into two stages: 1.Charging stage: When the low-side MOSFET is turned on, the source potential of the high-side MOSFET is pulled close to ground. The power supply charges the bootstrap capacitor through the bootstrap diode, causing the capacitor voltage to approach the supply voltage and storing the required energy. (Bootstrap capacitor charging) 2.Discharge and drive stage: After the low-side MOSFET turns off, the high-side source potential rises. The stored charge in the bootstrap capacitor raises the gate voltage to approximately “source voltage + supply voltage,” providing sufficient gate-source voltage to fully turn on the high-side MOSFET.At this point, the bootstrap diode becomes reverse-biased, preventing the high-voltage charge from flowing back into the preceding circuit and protecting the driver stage. (Bootstrap capacitor discharge) 3.3 Bootstrap Circuit Design Considerations The bootstrap capacitor continuously discharges while the high-side MOSFET is on, causing the gate-source voltage to gradually decrease. If the voltage becomes too low, the MOSFET may not turn on completely, resulting in increased power dissipation and heating. The following points should therefore be considered during design: Place the bootstrap capacitor close to the BOOT and SW pins of the gate driver IC. Keep the traces short and wide to minimize parasitic inductance. A Schottky diode is preferred for the bootstrap diode because it provides low forward voltage and low reverse-recovery losses. Avoid keeping the high-side MOSFET continuously on for an extended period. Make sure the capacitor has sufficient time to recharge during the switching cycle. Select an appropriate bootstrap capacitor value to balance drive duration and switching response. 4. PCB Layout Design Guidelines PCB Layout directly determines the electromagnetic compatibility, thermal performance, and operating reliability of an H-bridge circuit. It is a critical step in converting the circuit design into a practical hardware implementation. The main PCB Layout objectives are to minimize parasitic inductance in the power loop, optimize thermal paths, isolate high-power and low-level signals, and establish a low-impedance grounding system. 4.1 Overall Layout Principles The layout should follow the principles of functional partitioning and signal flow. The PCB can be divided into three independent areas: the power section, driver section, and logic control section. Power section: Place MOSFETs, freewheeling diodes, input filtering capacitors, current-sense resistors, and other high-current components close to the motor output connector to shorten the power path. Driver section: Place the gate driver IC, bootstrap circuit, and gate resistors close to the power MOSFETs to minimize the gate-drive loop. Logic section: Place the MCU, interface circuits, sensing circuits, and other low-power components away from high-current switching nodes to prevent noise coupling. 4.2 Power Loop Design The power loop is one of the main sources of parasitic inductance and switching noise. The key design objective is to minimize the loop area. Keep the core loop compact: The main power loop consists of: Power input → high-side MOSFET → motor → low-side MOSFET → ground → input capacitor. The loop area should be kept as small as possible. Arrange the MOSFETs closely together and avoid long traces and unnecessary bends. High-current routing: Use wide copper traces or copper pours for high-current paths. With 1 oz copper, a current-carrying capacity of approximately 1 A/mm of trace width can be used as a basic estimate. Where appropriate, use both the top and bottom copper layers and connect them with stitching vias to reduce impedance and inductance. Place filtering capacitors close to the power devices: Large electrolytic capacitors should be paralleled with high-frequency ceramic capacitors and placed close to the MOSFET source pins. Keep the distance within 0.5 cm. Connect the capacitor pads directly to the power and ground planes using multiple vias to minimize parasitic effects introduced by traces. 4.3 Gate-Drive Loop Design Parasitic parameters in the gate-drive loop can affect switching speed and may even cause gate oscillation. The following design requirements should be met: Keep the trace from the gate driver output pin to the MOSFET gate as short and straight as possible. The recommended length is within 1 cm, with a trace width of approximately 15–20 mil. Place the gate series resistor and gate pull-down resistor close to the MOSFET gate pin to suppress switching oscillation. Connect the return path of the gate-drive signal directly to the corresponding MOSFET source to avoid ground-bounce noise caused by a long shared ground path. Avoid routing gate-drive traces parallel to power traces for long distances. Maintain a spacing of at least 3 mm to reduce coupling interference. 4.4 Grounding and EMC Design Grounding is critical for suppressing electromagnetic interference and preventing ground-bounce noise. Separate grounds with a single-point connection: Divide the system ground into power ground (PGND) and signal ground (DGND/AGND). Power ground carries high-current switching loops, while signal ground is used only for logic and sensing circuits. Connect the two grounds at a single point near the input filtering capacitor to prevent voltage drops caused by high currents in the ground plane from affecting sensitive signals. Keep this trace short and minimize its copper area to prevent antenna effects. Sensitive signal traces and crystal oscillator traces should be routed away from this area. Where necessary, surround the sensitive traces with ground traces for additional shielding. 4.5 Thermal Design MOSFETs and freewheeling diodes are the main heat-generating components. Copper-pour cooling: Connect the MOSFET source, drain, and thermal pads to large copper areas to provide the primary heat dissipation path. Filled vias or copper-filled vias can further improve thermal conductivity. Reserve space for heat sinks: For high-power applications, reserve mounting holes and sufficient space for a heat sink. Use thermal grease or thermal pads between the device and heat sink. Thermally symmetrical layout: When multiple devices are connected in parallel or the bridge arms are arranged symmetrically, ensure that their thermal paths are also balanced to prevent localized overheating. 5. Overview of H-Bridge Drive Circuits An H-bridge drive circuit is one of the most widely used basic topologies in DC motor drive systems. Its core structure consists of four independently controlled MOSFETs arranged as a bridge. By controlling different switching combinations, the circuit can control the current direction and achieve forward rotation, reverse rotation, speed control, and braking of a DC motor. The topology resembles the letter “H,” which is where the name H-bridge comes from. This article provides a systematic analysis of the key considerations in H-bridge circuit design, covering device characteristics, high-side driving principles, bootstrap circuit design, and PCB Layout guidelines. It focuses on the essential aspects from circuit design to board-level implementation, providing practical guidance for DC motor driver design and optimization. (H-Bridge Circuit Topology) 2. Key Device Characteristics and Selection 2.1 MOSFET Body Diode Characteristics Inside an N-channel power MOSFET, the source and drain are N-type semiconductor regions, while the body region is made of P-type semiconductor material. This structure forms two PN junctions. Since the source is normally shorted to the body, the source-body PN junction remains at zero bias and does not function as a diode. Only the drain-body PN junction operates normally, forming the built-in body diode. This characteristic is common to power MOSFETs and is also the physical basis for the reverse-parallel diode shown in MOSFET symbols used in circuit simulation models. 2.2 Function and Selection of Freewheeling Diodes A DC motor is a typical inductive load, meaning that its current cannot change instantaneously. When the MOSFETs in an H-bridge switch rapidly between states, sudden changes in the motor winding current can generate high-voltage back-EMF spikes, which may damage the MOSFETs or cause abnormal circuit operation. A freewheeling diode is connected in parallel with the MOSFET drain and source. Its main functions include: Providing a freewheeling path: When the MOSFET turns off, the diode provides a closed-loop path for the residual current in the motor winding, preventing high-voltage spikes caused by forced current interruption. Protecting the devices from overvoltage: The diode clamps the back-EMF amplitude and isolates the power devices from voltage spikes, reducing the risk of device damage. Improving electromagnetic performance: In high-frequency switching applications, the diode helps suppress electromagnetic interference (EMI), reduce operating noise, and improve system stability. The MOSFET's built-in body diode can provide basic freewheeling functionality, but its relatively high forward voltage, long reverse-recovery time, and slow switching response make it unsuitable for high-frequency and high-current applications. In practical designs, an external Schottky diode is commonly connected in parallel as a dedicated freewheeling device. Its short reverse-recovery time and low forward voltage can significantly reduce freewheeling losses and improve circuit reliability. Continuous drain current (ID): The rating should exceed both the motor's rated current and stall current, with additional margin based on the thermal design. On-resistance (RDS(on)): This parameter directly determines conduction losses and device heating. For MOSFETs with the same voltage rating, a lower RDS(on) generally results in higher system efficiency. Gate charge (Qg): This parameter reflects MOSFET switching characteristics. A lower Qg generally results in lower switching losses, but it must be properly matched to the driving capability of the gate driver IC. 3. Its potential changes dynamically with the switching state and remains above ground. As a result, a conventional drive voltage cannot provide sufficient gate-source voltage. A dedicated circuit is required to generate a gate-drive voltage higher than the supply voltage. Verify Now Blog > Industrial-Grade RS-485 Communication Interface Design and PCB Layout Industrial-Grade RS-485 Communication Interface Design and PCB Layout by: Mila Aug 18,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout rs485 pcb 1. Introduction: An Irreplaceable Foundation of Industrial Bus Communication In industrial automation, medical equipment, and smart grid applications, the stability of communication interfaces directly determines the reliability and operational lifespan of the entire system. Although Ethernet and various wireless communication technologies have become increasingly widespread, the RS-485 standard, approved by the Electronic Industries Association (EIA) in 1983, remains a mainstream industrial interface standard due to its outstanding cost-effectiveness and unparalleled resistance to common-mode interference. Many higher-level communication standards even explicitly define RS-485 as the reference physical layer standard, such as China's electricity meter communication protocol standard DL/T645. The widespread adoption of RS-485 Modbus communication in industrial bus control systems is mainly attributed to the following key electrical characteristics of RS-485: Differential Signal Transmission: Unlike the single-ended signaling used by RS-232, RS-485 transmits differential signals through two wires (A and B). Electromagnetic interference from the surrounding environment is typically coupled equally onto both signal lines in the form of common-mode noise. Since a differential receiver is only sensitive to the voltage difference between the two lines, it effectively rejects common-mode noise, providing the system with exceptional noise immunity and strong resistance to interference. Powerful Multi-Point Communication Capability: The traditional RS-485 standard allows up to 32 unit loads (Unit Load, UL) to be connected on the same bus. With advances in semiconductor technology, modern RS-485 transceivers typically feature reduced unit loads (for example, 1/8 UL), enabling up to 256 nodes to be connected to a single bus without the need for additional repeaters. Long-Distance Communication and Flexible Data Rates: At a data rate of 100 kbps, RS-485 can theoretically support a maximum cable transmission distance of up to 4,000 feet (approximately 1,200 meters). For shorter distances (such as 40 feet), the maximum data rate can increase significantly, reaching up to 10 Mbps. Modern high-speed interface circuits can even operate at data rates of up to 40 Mbps. Half-Duplex Communication Mode: In the most common two-wire RS-485 network, data transmission and reception cannot occur simultaneously. This requires all nodes to strictly control bus access through direction control signals (such as the Driver Enable signal). Proper software coordination is necessary to prevent data collisions and bus contention caused by multiple drivers attempting to access the bus at the same time. Note: Full-duplex and half-duplex bus structures in RS-485. 2. Electrical Parameters and Physical Layer Network Topology 2.1 Signal Levels and Noise Margin Design It is important to clarify that RS-485 is only an electrical standard for the physical layer. It defines the electrical characteristics of drivers and receivers in a balanced multi-point transmission line, but it does not specify any higher-level communication protocols. Regarding signal levels, an RS-485-compliant driver is capable of providing a differential output voltage of no less than 1.5 V across a 54 Ω load. On the receiving end, a standard RS-485 receiver features extremely high sensitivity and can accurately detect differential input signals as low as 200 mV. The large voltage margin between the transmitter output level of 1.5 V and the receiver detection threshold of 200 mV provides substantial tolerance for signal attenuation caused by long-distance cable transmission. This is one of the fundamental reasons why RS-485 can operate reliably in harsh industrial environments with significant electrical noise. Note: Minimum bus signal level specified by the RS-485 standard. 2.2 Daisy-Chain Topology and Stub Length Control To minimize high-frequency signal reflections on the transmission line, the RS-485 standard strongly recommends using a daisy-chain topology to connect network nodes (also known as a bus topology). This topology requires drivers and receivers to be connected to the main bus through extremely short “stubs” and should avoid star or tree-type branching structures whenever possible. The electrical length of the stub (the distance between the transceiver and the main cable trunk) must be strictly controlled. Theoretically, it should be less than one-tenth of the driver output rise time. The formula is as follows: L_Stub ≤ (tr / 10) × v × c where tr is the rise time, v is the signal velocity factor, and c is the speed of light. Therefore, for industrial applications that require relatively long stubs, selecting transceivers with slower rise times (i.e., slew-rate-limited drivers) is a practical and effective approach. This not only improves signal integrity but also reduces EMI (electromagnetic interference) generated by the device. 3. Advanced Hardware Design: Termination, Fault Protection, and Isolation 3.1 Bus Termination and Common-Mode Noise Filtering The data transmission line must always be properly terminated to eliminate signal reflections. Since industrial RS-485 cables (such as 22–24 AWG twisted-pair cables) typically have a characteristic impedance (Z<sub>0</sub>) of approximately 120 Ω, a 120 Ω termination resistor is normally placed at each end of the bus. In high-noise industrial environments, a more advanced termination design replaces the single 120 Ω resistor with two 60 Ω resistors, with a 220 pF capacitor connected to ground at the midpoint, forming a low-pass filter. This configuration provides additional common-mode noise filtering capability. However, 1% precision resistors must be used in this design. Otherwise, resistor mismatch can convert common-mode noise into harmful differential-mode noise, potentially causing communication failures. Note: Proper RS-485 bus termination. 3.2 Failsafe Protection for Idle Bus States In industrial environments, three conditions can cause the differential input signal to drop to zero momentarily: cable disconnection (open circuit), insulation damage (short circuit), or all nodes remaining in an idle waiting state. Traditional RS-485 receivers may produce an unpredictable output state when the input voltage is 0 V. To force the receiver to output a defined logic-high state when the signal is lost, an external failsafe biasing circuit must be implemented. A common approach is to pull the A line up to the supply voltage and pull the B line down to ground. To ensure sufficient noise margin, the differential voltage generated by the bias network must exceed the receiver’s 200 mV input threshold while also providing adequate margin against maximum differential noise. For example, using two 523 Ω pull-up and pull-down resistors together with a 120 Ω termination resistor can establish a robust biasing circuit that ensures reliable bus operation. Note: External idle bus fail safe biasing circuit. 3.3 Ground Potential Difference (GPD) and System-Level Isolation Solutions This is an easily overlooked trap. Since remote nodes may draw power from electrical equipment in different facilities, significant Ground Potential Differences (GPD) can occur between system grounds. These voltage differences can be superimposed onto the cable as common-mode interference. If the system relies solely on local ground as the current return path, or directly connects remote grounds through a grounding wire, the resulting large ground loop currents can severely disrupt the signal. The truly robust solution capable of tolerating ground potential differences of several kilovolts is signal and power supply isolation. By using DC/DC converters (power isolation) and digital capacitive isolators (signal isolation), ground loop currents can be completely eliminated. Note: Isolation of two remote transceiver stations with a single ground reference. 4. Typical Practical Case: Development of an Isolated USB-to-RS-485 Module Combining all the design theories discussed above, we will analyze a highly reliable isolated USB-to-RS-485 module that is widely used in engineering debugging environments. As a host-side device connected to a PC, the module must not only protect the expensive PC motherboard from being damaged by industrial surges but also ensure zero packet loss during communication. 4.1 System Topology and Isolation Boundary Definition The system data flow is clearly defined as: USB Interface → USB-to-UART Bridge Chip (such as FT232 / CH340) → Isolation Barrier → RS-485 Transceiver → Bus Side The module breaks the electrical connection at the logic level (UART TTL) and uses a dual-channel high-speed digital isolation chip to safely transfer signals across the isolation barrier. This topology not only keeps the complex USB protocol stack within the safe zone but also reduces the cost of the isolator. 4.2 Isolated Power Supply Design Details The isolated transceiver on the RS-485 bus side requires an independent and clean 5V power supply. In this design, the 5V power is extracted from the motherboard USB VBUS and used to drive a transformer-based push-pull DC/DC isolated power module. At the schematic level, considering that the RS-485 transceiver generates significant transient switching currents when driving long cables and 32 nodes, the output side of the DC/DC module should not only include conventional 100 nF high-frequency decoupling capacitors but also require a nearby 10 μF low-ESR tantalum capacitor or a ceramic capacitor array connected in parallel to serve as a local energy reservoir. 4.3 PCB Layout: Creepage Distance and High-Voltage Immunity During the PCB layout stage, the success of the isolation design completely depends on the clearance zone. A physical isolation gap of at least 2.5 mm to 5 mm must be maintained between the primary-side ground (USB digital ground) and the secondary-side ground (RS-485 isolated ground). In multilayer PCBs, all inner layers (including power and ground planes) directly beneath this isolation gap must also be strictly cleared. No traces are allowed to cross this area to prevent high-voltage arcing, creepage, or layer-to-layer breakdown. To further improve voltage withstand capability, a slot can be physically milled into the PCB at the boundary between the two ground planes. 4.4 Multi-Level Surge and ESD Protection Layout Strategy for Interfaces For the A/B interface used in harsh industrial environments, a three-stage protection scheme is configured in the schematic: the primary Gas Discharge Tube (GDT) absorbs high-energy surges, the secondary Polymeric Positive Temperature Coefficient (PTC) fuse provides overcurrent protection, and the final-stage Transient Voltage Suppressor (TVS) performs precise voltage clamping. During PCB layout, the physical order of “progressive eFnergy discharge” must be strictly followed. Signals entering from the external connector must first pass through the GDT pads, then go through the PTC, and finally reach the TVS before connecting to the transceiver pins. A “via-based lead” star routing structure must never be used. At the same time, the TVS ground pin must be connected to the isolation ground plane through extremely short and wide traces or multiple vias to ensure an ultra-low discharge impedance path. Note: PCB 3D simulation view. 5. Conclusion RS-485 interface design is a system engineering discipline that appears simple but is actually highly sophisticated. From selecting the appropriate network topology and implementing proper termination for long-distance transmission, to achieving system isolation against ground potential differences, and finally to controlling routing order and clearance requirements during PCB layout, every aspect is closely interconnected. Only by deeply understanding the physical principles behind the standard and properly applying modern isolation and protection components can engineers build a robust and reliable industrial communication link capable of operating in complex electromagnetic environments.
